***

Every four minutes, a life ends in New York State. 

To hell with you and your poetry—you will rot and be blown through the next solar system alongside the rest of the cosmic gases. What on earth do you know about it? 

Consider these fundamental axioms: Avoid getting killed. Observe the Careful Crossing Campaign. Cross crossings cautiously. 

Meanwhile, horses—black and white—prance by. 

What is the point of sweating over this sort of thing, Carl, when it is already all laid out for us? 

Consider the outings available in New York City: venture out into the open country rather than remaining confined in sweltering rooms. Escape to one of the Great Parks—Pelham Bay, for example. Situated along the Long Island Sound, it offers bathing, boating, tennis, baseball, golf, and more. Discover acres upon acres of lush green grass, magnificent shade trees, and rippling brooks. Simply board the Pelham Bay Park Branch of the Lexington Avenue (East Side) Line, and you will arrive in just a few minutes. 

— *Brought to you by the Interborough Rapid Transit Company*

***

### Life, Danger, and Deliverance in the Urban Grid

The modern city is a place of stark contrasts, where the fragile nature of human existence is routinely weighed against the indifferent machinery of urban life. In New York State, cold statistics reveal a grim rhythm: a human life comes to an end every four minutes. This harsh reality sits in tension with a broader, almost existential dismissal of human life and art—a cynical worldview that reduces the fleeting beauty of poetry and individual existence to mere background noise in a vast, unfeeling metropolis. 

Yet, amidst this implicit fatalism, the city actively struggles to keep its citizens alive. On the crowded pavement, daily survival requires constant vigilance. The "Careful Crossing Campaign" serves as a stark, ubiquitous reminder of the dangers lurking at every intersection, using public safety slogans to urge pedestrians to navigate the chaotic street crossings with extreme caution. In a landscape where a moment’s distraction can prove fatal, the simple act of walking across a street becomes a deliberate negotiation between life and death.

Beyond the immediate physical hazards of traffic, the suffocating environment of the city presents its own quiet toll. During the oppressive heat of the summer months, urban residents find themselves trapped in sweltering, airless indoor rooms. Recognizing this collective misery, pervasive advertisements urge city dwellers to break free from their concrete enclosures. These campaigns market a vital antidote to urban fatigue: refreshing outings to the open countryside and the expansive green refuges of New York City’s great park system.

Among these advertised sanctuaries, Pelham Bay Park stands out as a premier destination for escape and renewal. Boasting vast stretches of unspoiled natural scenery, the park offers a striking antidote to the claustrophobic grid of the city. Visitors can immerse themselves in a wide array of outdoor recreational activities, from organized sports to peaceful strolls. Most invitingly, its location along the shores of the Long Island Sound provides ample opportunities for boating and refreshing aquatic bathing, transforming the waterfront into a summer playground for the weary public.

Reaching this coastal haven is made remarkably simple through the city's expanding infrastructure. The Interborough Rapid Transit Company aggressively promotes its services, advertising fast, direct, and convenient transit to Pelham Bay Park via the Lexington Avenue Line. Through this seamless connection, the very transit system that shuttles workers through the stressful heart of the city also serves as the ultimate line of deliverance—carrying residents away from the threats, heat, and existential noise of the streets to the healing waters of the coast.
outputs.L4:
Iron screeching on iron. The subterranean dark of the Interborough Rapid Transit shattered by sudden, strobing bursts of yellow tungsten light. 14th Street. Change for the Brooklyn Express.

*WATCH THE GAP. WATCH YOUR STEP. DO NOT LEAN AGAINST THE DOORS.*

A wall of hot damp air, thick with the stench of ozone, coal smoke, and wet wool, surged through the opened doors. A sea of wool caps and felt fedoras surged inward, a single collective organism writhing toward the cane-webbed seats.

"I sometimes wonder," she murmured, her gloves clutching the greasy brass handrail, her eyes fixed on the black tunnel beyond, "if any of us are actually going anywhere. Or if we just ride this iron loop until the spring winds down and we’re tossed onto the slag heap."

*BUY PALMOLIVE SOAP FOR THAT SCHOOLGIRL COMPLEXION! KEEP THAT YOUTHFUL GLOW!*

"Did you hear about old man Miller?" a voice croaked from beneath the rim of a stained bowler. "Fell right through the floorboards of the Third Avenue El. Crushed his ribs. Died before the ambulance could cross Bowery."

*SPITTING IS PROHIBITED BY LAW. VIOLATORS WILL BE FINED $500 OR IMPRISONED. PREVENT THE SPREAD OF CONSUMPTION.*

*TONIGHT AT THE PALACE! THE ZIEGFELD FOLLIES! DANCING GIRLS! SPARKLING COMEDY! FORGET YOUR TROUBLES IN A PARADISE OF LIGHTS!*

The train lurched, throwing shoulder against shoulder, flesh against flesh. A thousand heartbeats hammering out a staccato syncopation against the deafening roar of the iron wheels. A neon sign flashed through the soot-stained glass of the car window: a gigantic, glowing bottle of Dr. Bell’s Pine-Tar Honey, dripping golden light over the dark silhouette of tenement fire escapes.

"He said to me, 'What's the point of saving a nickel a day?'" a young woman said, her voice swallowed instantly by the screech of the brakes. "'What’s a nickel buy when the meat is rotten and the baby has the croup?'"

*TAKE A VACATION IN SUNNY BERMUDA! STEAMSHIP TICKETS ON SALE NOW! ESCAPE THE COLD!*

*DANGER: HIGH VOLTAGE. DO NOT TOUCH THE THIRD RAIL. INSTANT DEATH.*

A newspaper rustled open in the crowd, its black ink smudging on sweat-slick thumbs. Headlines flickered past like telephone poles out a window: *MINE DISASTER KILLS 40 IN PENNSYLVANIA... GERMAN MARK COLLAPSES... MYSTERY WOMAN FOUND DROWNED IN EAST RIVER.*

"Look at that poster, Clara," a man said, pointing a nicotine-stained finger toward the ceiling curved above the strap-hangers. "She’s got a smile on her, hasn't she? Like she doesn't know the whole damn city is built on top of graves."

*SMOKE LUCKY STRIKES—IT’S TOASTED! DOES NOT IRRITATE THE THROAT!*

*BEWARE OF PICKPOCKETS. KEEP YOUR HAND ON YOUR WATCH.*

The light flickered out, plunging the car into a brief, suffocating darkness. In the blackness, thirty lungs inhaled as one, holding a collective breath against the void. The smell of scorched rubber and cheap perfume hung heavy in the air. For three seconds, the universe reduced itself to the blind, rhythmic pounding of steel on steel, a relentless machine carrying its silent, terrifying freight of mortal souls through the bedrock of Manhattan.

Then the lights flared back to life.

*USE PEPSODENT TO REMOVE THE FILM ON YOUR TEETH! BRIGHTEN YOUR SMILE TODAY!*

The conductor's voice tore through the car like a rusty saw: "Times Square! Next stop, Times Square! Step lively, folks, step lively!"
outputs.L5:
In a city where millions of lives intersect on concrete grids, **New** **York** has always held a singular, magnetic promise: the chance to become **somebody**.

Step off the train at Grand Central or emerge from the subway into the amber glow of a Manhattan dusk, and you can feel it immediately—the urgent, pulsing energy of a place built on reinvention. Here, history is etched into the shadows of glass skyscrapers, and the avenues are paved with the quiet ambitions of those who left somewhere else behind to chase a dream.

In **New** **York**, identity is a captivating paradox. You can easily exist as an anonymous face in the crowd, blending into the tide of commuters crossing the Brooklyn Bridge. Yet, the city simultaneously makes you feel visible, as if every neon sign and brownstone doorstep is a backdrop for your own story. It is a place that tests your resolve, stripping away the familiar and asking a simple, relentless question: *Who are you going to be?*

To be **somebody** in **New** **York** doesn't necessarily mean seeing your name in lights over Broadway or occupying a high-rise office above Wall Street. Sometimes, it simply means finding your voice amidst the roar of the traffic. It means standing on a rainy street corner, watching the yellow cabs blur past, and realizing that you have carved out your own resilient space in the center of the world.

Every morning, the sun rises over the East River, washing the brick and steel in a **new** light, offering eight million people the chance to start fresh. And as long as the city keeps beating to its relentless rhythm, there will always be dreamers walking its streets, looking up at the sky, ready to prove that they, too, are **somebody**.

**SUBTERRANEAN ELECTRIC: 1923**

DROP FIVE CENTS IN THE SLOT.
The iron mouth consumes the nickel.

*Pond’s Vanishing Cream—*
*For the complexion of perpetual youth.*
Beneath Forty-Second Street, youth is a film of soot.
The tunnel smells of damp limestone and ozone.
A million eyes staring through the glass at nothing.

WATCH YOUR STEP.
  WATCH YOUR STEP.
    WATCH YOUR—

*UNEEDA BISCUIT.*
In crisp, moisture-proof packages.
Spitting on the platform is strictly forbidden by law.
Fine: Five dollars, or thirty days in the tombs.
(The soul, too, is easily dried and swept onto the tracks.)

*Lucky Strike—It’s Toasted.*
No throat irritation. No cough.
The third rail hums its one-note hymn,
sixty cycles of absolute, indifferent light.
BEWARE OF PICKPOCKETS.
They will take your pocket watch.
The train will take the rest.

*Gillette Safety Razor: No Stropping, No Honing.*
A smooth shave for the morning rush.
A clean chin for the open coffin.
The turnstile clicks: 
*one, one, one, one—*
a census of the damned, numbered in brass teeth.

DO NOT LEAN AGAINST THE DOORS.
THEY MAY OPEN AT ANY TIME.

*Wrigley’s Spearmint keeps the flavor long!*
Chew away the taste of pulverized iron.
Chew away the sound of your father dying in Ohio.
*Wear Holeproof Hosiery—Guaranteed for Six Months.*
It will outlast the flesh inside it.

ELECTRIC CURRENT: DANGER. 600 VOLTS.
Do not touch the live steel.
Do not look directly into the eyes of the man across the aisle.
He knows where this train ends.

*DRINK MOXIE! DISTINCTLY DIFFERENT.*
Step back behind the white line.
Step back.
Step—

The express passes without stopping.
A blur of lit windows,
stuffed with yellow newsprint,
and faces that have already forgotten their names.

BUY A DIAMOND ON CREDIT.
PAY AS YOU EARN.
Eternity arranged in small, weekly installments.

FALLING FROM THE PLATFORM IS FATAL.
*(Passengers are requested to remain calm while the wreckage is cleared.)*

**DYNAMIC METROPOLIS: BULLETIN NO. 9**

Step lively! 
The Municipal Rapid Transit Line extends its iron tendrils—
FORTY THOUSAND YARDS OF REINFORCED CONCRETE!
A glowing, grid-work promise of 100% Efficiency!
Look up, citizen! The sky is a blueprint!
The steam-shovel sings the aria of Modernity!
*Electric! Pneumatic! Chrome-plated Progress!*

(And under the asphalt, Carl, 
the lime breaks down the hip-bone. 
The worm doesn't need a transfer ticket. 
It eats the mayor; it eats the motorman; 
it eats the blueprint whole.)

Look at your city of broad shoulders, Carl!
You sit there with your hair over one eye,
tugging your suspenders, writing odes to the wheat and the smokestacks,
fooling the clerks into thinking their sweat smells like laurels.
"Hog Butcher for the World," you sang—
well, who buys the offal, Carl?
Who scrapes the gristle off the tracks at 4:00 AM?
Your "tool maker" has a cough like a crushed tin can.
Your "player with railroads" is getting buried in a cardboard box
beneath the very switchyard he oiled last Tuesday.

AUTOMATIC SANITATION! 
PURE MOUNTAIN WATER BROUGHT THROUGH 90 MILES OF RIVETED STEEL PIPELINE!
VOTE YES ON THE SEWER BOND!

A gleaming, hygienic future for our children!
(Until the soil claims them, Carl.
Until their eyes turn to grey jelly in the dark.
No incandescent bulb lights the six-foot trench.
No elevator rises from that basement.)

You soft-headed romantic of the stockyards—
you think the whistle blows for *life*?
It’s a factory for rot, Carl!
The skyscraper is just a tall headstone with telegraph wires.
We pave over the dead,
we set up a soda fountain on their dust,
and we call it a PARADISE OF COMMERCE!

Clang-clang goes the trolley—
Rattle-rattle goes the jawbone—

*Buy a lot in the New Annex today!*
*(Ground guaranteed deep enough to hide the stench.)*

I.

Glazed terracotta, IRT monogram in relief:  
*The Quickest Way Across the City.*  
1928: *Avoid the Surface Delay.*  
*Ride Below the Dust and Heat.*  
Rattan seats, mahogany window sash,  
nickel-plated stanchions.  
A single coin buys twenty miles of track.  

II.

The pneumatic hammer strikes cold asphalt above.  
*Rat-tat-tat-tat-tat.*  
Below, the wheel flange bites the turn at 14th.  
A high, dry screech—  
steel against raw steel at ninety decibels.  
Rust flakes from the cross-beam,  
drops to the ballast stone.  
Air pushed through the iron street-grate:  
smell of ozone, brake shoe, wet granite.  

III.

STAND BACK FROM THE PLATFORM EDGE.  
The stencil wears thin on the yellow band.  
DO NOT LEAN AGAINST THE DOORS.  
WALK, DO NOT RUN.  
The third rail: six hundred volts direct current.  
DANGER: LIVE RAIL.  
KEEP HANDS CLEAR.  
REPORT UNATTENDED PACKAGES.  

IV.

*Modern Steel Cars for Modern New Yorkers,*  
printed on cardstock, set in an enamel frame  
beside an advertisement for pomade.  
The 10:14 express passes without stopping.  
A wall of displaced wind.  
WATCH THE GAP.  
The boot tip pauses six inches above the void.  
The tungsten bulb flickers off.  
The tungsten bulb flickers on.  
The red tail-lights pull down the bore.
